opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I've always had a pretty simple filter for what I want to spend my time on. It has to be something that matters a lot if it works, something that's genuinely hard, and something where I have some unfair advantage, some reason to think I'm well positioned to make progress where others haven't. Smell checks all three boxes for me.

On the "matters" side: smell is everywhere and almost totally undigitized. We have cameras and microphones in our pockets. Vision and hearing have been turned into data, and that's unlocked enormous amounts of science and technology. But smell, which is tied to our food, our health, our memories, how we choose partners, how insects find us and spread disease, has basically no digital representation. There's no "RGB" for odor. So if you can crack that, you open up a whole new sensory dimension for computing, and the applications range from flavors and fragrances to agriculture to medical diagnostics.

On the "hard" side: the core scientific problem is that we can't predict what a molecule smells like from its structure. It's been an open question for a very long time. Molecules that look nearly identical can smell completely different, and molecules that look nothing alike can smell the same. The receptor biology is complicated: we have hundreds of olfactory receptor types, and they respond combinatorially. It's a problem where classical approaches stalled out.

And then the third piece, the personal one: I've been obsessed with olfaction since I was a teenager. I did my PhD in neuroscience, studying behavior and the brain, and then I spent years in machine learning, at Twitter and at Google Brain. So I happened to sit at this intersection where modern machine learning, especially graph neural networks that can operate directly on molecular structure, finally became a good fit for a problem I'd cared about for most of my life. When you find something that's important, unsolved, and where your weird background is actually an asset, that's when I think you should go all in.

r001.rationale: The response says smell is largely undigitized and the problem is difficult and long unsolved, but it does not identify a scarcity of people working on digital smell as a reason Alex is drawn to it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I've had this kind of personal rubric for a long time about what's worth spending a career on. And it's basically three questions. Is it important? Is it hard? And is it solvable in my lifetime? And the thing about olfaction is that it checks all three boxes in a way that very few problems do.

On the importance side, smell is one of the most fundamental senses we have. It's how all living things, from single-celled organisms to us, have detected chemicals in the environment for the entire history of life. It's tied to memory, to emotion, to disease detection, to food, to safety. And yet we've digitized sight and we've digitized sound, and those have transformed the world, but we haven't digitized smell. There's this entire dimension of reality that computers are completely blind to. So the opportunity there is enormous.

On the hard side, it's really hard. Vision has this nice structure, you've got wavelengths of light, it's basically a one-dimensional spectrum. Sound is pressure waves over time. Smell is molecules. There are tens of billions of possible odorous molecules, and the relationship between a molecule's structure and what it smells like is incredibly non-obvious. Two molecules that look almost identical on paper can smell completely different, and molecules that look nothing alike can smell the same. People have been trying to crack that for over a century and it's resisted them.

And then the solvable part is what changed in the last decade or so. Machine learning got good enough that you could start to learn that mapping from structure to perception, and the sensor hardware and the biology have matured to the point where you can actually start building the whole stack. So when I was at Google Brain, and now with what we're doing at Osmo, it felt like the first moment in history where this problem went from being a scientific curiosity to something you could actually make real progress on. And when something is that important, that hard, and finally tractable, I think you kind of have an obligation to go after it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes smell as important, difficult, and newly tractable, but does not say that few other people work on giving computers a sense of smell or identify that scarcity as a reason for Alex’s interest.

astra-6.text:
For me, it sits at the intersection of a fundamental scientific question and something that could be useful in the world. Smell is this very familiar experience, but the relationship between a molecule and what we perceive is still remarkably hard to explain. How does a chemical structure become the smell of a rose or a cup of coffee? Can we learn that mapping well enough to predict it?

And then there’s the engineering opportunity. We’ve given computers ways to capture and interpret images and sound, but we don’t have an equivalent, general-purpose way to capture and interpret smell. If we could build that, we’d have access to a whole layer of information about the physical world that’s currently difficult to use.

That combination is what draws me in: a deep question, a technical challenge where machine learning might make a difference, and the possibility of turning the answer into something useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes smell as a difficult scientific and engineering problem, but does not say that few other people are working on giving computers a sense of smell.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, work worth pursuing sits at the intersection of a really interesting scientific question and something that could make a meaningful difference in people’s lives. Smell has both of those qualities. It’s this fundamental sense that we use every day, but we understand it much less well than vision or hearing. We can record an image or a sound and send it across the world. We don’t have an equivalent way to capture and reproduce a smell.

And there’s a really compelling machine learning problem underneath that: How do you go from the structure of a molecule to what somebody experiences when they smell it? If we can build that connection, we can start giving computers access to a whole category of information they’ve largely been missing. That opens up possibilities in health, in food, in understanding our environment. It’s a deep scientific problem where making progress could also be useful, and that combination is very motivating to me.

r001.rationale: The response says smell is less understood than vision or hearing and lacks a way to capture and reproduce it, but it does not identify a scarcity of people working on computer smell as a reason Alex is drawn to it.
